text:
Done, and it found the C1 hole with hard evidence rather than argument.

Built a real cross-process harness: AtomicRaceWorker is a tiny main that performs one operation and prints WON or LOST:<typed failure>; AtomicCrossProcessSuite spawns 8 JVMs (java -cp from java.class.path, available because Test/fork is on), starts all of them BEFORE reading any output so they genuinely overlap, then counts outcomes. Five tests: publishOnce, writeNew, published-content-belongs-to-one-writer, writeStable idempotence, and claim of a contested source.

Result against the pre-C1 kernel, on macOS/APFS, reproduced on three consecutive runs:
  writeNew => "WON, WON, WON, LOST:TargetExists, LOST:TargetExists, ..."
Two or three winners EVERY run. Each winner believed it had published; the file holds one winner's bytes and the others were silently clobbered. The locked publishOnce won exactly once on every run, which is the control: it proves the sidecar lock genuinely serializes across processes and that the difference is the lock, not timing.

This is precisely what same-JVM fibers could never show. AtomicFiles serializes in-process callers through a striped monitor BEFORE the sidecar lock is contended, so an in-process test measures the monitor. And the pre-existing claim race moved one source toward DIFFERENT destinations, so it never contended a destination at all.

After C1 the suite passes 5/5 on three consecutive runs.

Filesystem qualification, which is the honest limit of this evidence: these results are macOS/APFS only. The failure mode depends on rename(2) replacing an existing target, which is POSIX behaviour and should reproduce on ext4, but NFS and Lustre lock and rename semantics remain unqualified. That qualification is C2's job and this harness is the tool for it.
